newsitem.title: UK: Felons can't, Di might vote in British election.
newsitem.headline: Felons can't, Di might vote in British election.

text.p: Queen Elizabeth wouldn't dream of it. Lords -- along with lunatics, felons and minors -- can't. Princess Diana might. And millions of citizens just won't bother to vote in Thursday's British election.
Considered the most fundamental right in democracies across the world, voting comes with its own idiosyncratic rules in Britain, where 44 million people are eligible.

Members of the House of Lords, along with under-18s, are forbidden to vote. So too are mental health patients, sentenced prisoners and those convicted within the last five years for corrupt or illegal election practices.

Britons living abroad have already voted by post -- and duly celebrated an end to the longest campaign for 80 years -- while Commonwealth and Irish citizens can join in the process if resident in Britain.
Some top royals are allowed to take part but most won't be exercising their right to determine Her Majesty's Government.
"The queen doesn't and royal dukes don't. Other members of the family are entitled to vote but it's up to them whether they wish to or not," said a Buckingham Palace spokeswoman.
Prince Charles, heir to the throne, cannot vote because he belongs to the House of Lords, parliament's upper house.
Most other high-profile members of the monarchy don't actually vote, as tradition dictates the royal family stay outside the dirty business of politics.
But younger royals might rebel against such niceties, just like they have broken so many other rules of royal life.
The divorced Duchess of York, Sarah "Fergie" Ferguson, is allowed to vote but is unlikely to as she has recently moved house and may not yet be registered in her new constituency.
No such problem plagues Diana, Princess of Wales, a millionaire mother of two who is heading into her first election since divorce from Prince Charles.
Diana can vote in the safest Conservative seat in the land: upmarket Kensington and Chelsea, where serial womaniser and outspoken Conservative rebel Alan Clark is all but sure to win.

A big hit with women -- he once bedded a judge's wife and both her daughters -- it is far from clear that Clark would win over Diana, who has already broken with tradition by appearing on a public platform with politicians.
An anti-establishmentarian when it suits her, Diana has enjoyed all the privileges that life at the top can offer but her political leanings are unclear.
Diana appears closer to the opposition Labour Party, favourite to win the election, on issues such as the homeless.

She caused consternation inside the ruling Conservative party by appearing to contradict its line on landmines during a high-profile overseas tour and has made enemies with some in government who count her ex-husband and his family as friends.
But officially at least, the new Diana is keeping quiet about the 1997 election.
"The princess is quite a private person when it comes to these things, as are most people in the country," said an aide.

"The princess is entitled to vote but as to where, when, how if and but -- I can't comment," she said. " I asked her just yesterday and she said it was a personal matter and she would like to keep it that way."

The question remains whether Diana -- schooled in the finer points of royal etiquette -- would know how to find the dingy church hall or musty school gymnasium used for the day's polling. Has she ever voted before?
"We didn't discuss it. Nobody in the office knows that," the aide replied.
